hmmt-feb-2012-team1-01.title: Congruent right triangles
hmmt-feb-2012-team1-01.body:
$D$ lies on the bisector of $\angle A$, so it is equidistant from lines $AB$ and $AC$: $DE=DF$. $D$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, so $DB=DC$. Triangles $DEB$ and $DFC$ have right angles at $E$ and $F$, equal hypotenuses $DB=DC$ and equal legs $DE=DF$, so they are congruent (hypotenuse-leg) and $BE=CF$. ∎

(The point $D$ exists as a single point only when $AB\ne AC$, since otherwise the two lines coincide.)

hmmt-feb-2012-team1-02.title: (a) Even $n$ exactly
hmmt-feb-2012-team1-02.body:
Call $i$ of *type 1* if $f(g(i))=i$ and of *type 2* if $g(f(i))=i$; by hypothesis every $i$ has exactly one type. Let $T_1,T_2$ be the sets of the two types.

If $i\in T_1$ and $j=g(i)$, then $g(f(j))=g(f(g(i)))=g(i)=j$, so $j$ has type 2 or both types; as exactly one type holds, $j\in T_2$. So $g$ maps $T_1$ into $T_2$, and it is injective on $T_1$ because $f(g(i))=i$ there. Hence $|T_1|\le|T_2|$. Symmetrically, if $i\in T_2$ and $j=f(i)$ then $f(g(j))=f(g(f(i)))=f(i)=j$, so $f$ maps $T_2$ injectively into $T_1$, and $|T_2|\le|T_1|$. So $|T_1|=|T_2|$ and $n=|T_1|+|T_2|$ is even.

For even $n$ take $f(2m-1)=f(2m)=2m-1$ and $g(2m-1)=g(2m)=2m$ for $m=1,\dots,\frac n2$. Then $f(g(2m-1))=f(2m)=2m-1$, $f(g(2m))=2m-1\ne2m$, $g(f(2m-1))=2m\ne2m-1$, $g(f(2m))=2m$, so exactly one condition holds for each $i$. So the answer to (a) is: all even $n$.

hmmt-feb-2012-team1-02.title: (b) Permutations: even $n\ge4$
hmmt-feb-2012-team1-02.body:
For permutations the same argument shows $n$ is even, and $T_1=\operatorname{Fix}(fg)$, $T_2=\operatorname{Fix}(gf)$ have size $\frac n2$ each, with $g(T_1)=T_2$. The permutation $fg$ fixes exactly the $\frac n2$ points of $T_1$, so it is a derangement on the other $\frac n2$ points. For $n=2$ that is impossible (a permutation of $2$ points that fixes one of them fixes both), so $n=2$ does not work.

For even $n=2m\ge4$: let $T_1=\{1,\dots,m\}$, $T_2=\{m+1,\dots,2m\}$, let $g$ swap $i\leftrightarrow m+i$, and let $\sigma$ be the permutation that fixes $T_1$ pointwise and acts as an $m$-cycle on $T_2$ (a derangement since $m\ge2$). Put $f=\sigma g^{-1}$, so $fg=\sigma$. Then $gf=g\sigma g^{-1}$ fixes exactly $g(T_1)=T_2$ and acts as an $m$-cycle on $g(T_2)=T_1$, with no fixed points there. So exactly one of $fg(i)=i$, $gf(i)=i$ holds for every $i$.

So for permutations the answer is: all even $n\ge4$ (and $n=2$ fails). (Confirmed by exhaustive search for $n\le6$.)

hmmt-feb-2012-team1-03.title: (a) Color argument
hmmt-feb-2012-team1-03.body: Color the board like a chessboard. Bob places both tokens on distinct squares of the same color. A move of either token (to an orthogonally adjacent square) changes the color of its square. After Alice's move her token is on the opposite color from Bob's, so the tokens are on different squares. Bob then moves; he has at least two neighbors available, so he can step to a neighbor that is not Alice's square, and now both tokens are on the same color again. By induction Alice never lands on Bob's square, and Bob never moves onto hers, so Bob survives all $2012$ rounds.

hmmt-feb-2012-team1-03.title: (b) Catch in at most 14 rounds
hmmt-feb-2012-team1-03.body:
Number the columns $1,\dots,8$ and the rows $1,\dots,8$; a king-type move can change the column by $-1,0,+1$ and the row by $-1,0,+1$ independently.

*Phase 1 (same column).* While Alice's column differs from Bob's, she moves one column toward Bob's column (and in any row direction). Bob's column changes by at most $1$ per move, so Alice's column index moves monotonically toward his and cannot pass his without equality occurring; since columns are between $1$ and $8$, within at most $7$ rounds the two tokens are in the same column (right after one of the moves).

*Phase 2 (same row).* From then on, on each of her moves Alice stays in Bob's column (she can, since his column changes by at most $1$) and moves one row toward Bob's row. If Alice is below Bob, her row index increases by $1$ each round and can never pass Bob's row without landing on his square (Bob moves at most one row per round); since rows are between $1$ and $8$, within at most $7$ rounds Alice's token is on Bob's square, and she wins.

So Alice wins within $14<2012$ rounds, whatever Bob does.

hmmt-feb-2012-team1-04.title: Coordinates and power of the point $M$
hmmt-feb-2012-team1-04.body:
Put $M=(0,0)$ with $l$ the $x$-axis, $A=(0,a)$ with $a>0$, $B=(u,v)$, $C=(-u,-v)$. Since $AB\ne AC$ we have $v\ne0$ (if $v=0$, then $B,C$ lie on $l$ and $A$ is on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$).

Line $AB$ meets the $x$-axis at $X=\left(\frac{au}{a-v},0\right)$ and line $AC$ at $Y=\left(\frac{-au}{a+v},0\right)$ (if $a=\pm v$ one of them is at infinity and $XBYC$ is not a quadrilateral). The lines $XY$ and $BC$ meet at $M$, so by the converse of the power of a point theorem, $X,B,Y,C$ are concyclic iff the signed products agree: $\overline{MX}\cdot\overline{MY}=\overline{MB}\cdot\overline{MC}$. Here
$$\overline{MX}\cdot\overline{MY}=-\frac{a^2u^2}{a^2-v^2},\qquad\overline{MB}\cdot\overline{MC}=-(u^2+v^2).$$
So $XBYC$ is cyclic $\iff a^2u^2=(u^2+v^2)(a^2-v^2)\iff v^2\left(a^2-u^2-v^2\right)=0\iff a^2=u^2+v^2$ (as $v\ne0$) $\iff MA=MB=MC$.

Finally $MA=MB=MC$ means $M$, the midpoint of $BC$, is the circumcenter of $ABC$ with $A$ on the circle with diameter $BC$, which holds iff $\angle BAC=90^\circ$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2012-team1-05.title: Only the five single-topping pizzas work
hmmt-feb-2012-team1-05.body:
Let $L$ be the set of toppings Arno likes. For each pizza $P_i$ (a set of toppings), Arno's answer is "yes" exactly when $P_i\not\subseteq L$. Purineqa must be able to determine $L$ from the five answers (the sixth pizza must be exactly $L$), so the map $L\mapsto$ (answers) must be injective on the $32$ subsets of toppings.

**Claim.** The five pizzas must be the five different single-topping pizzas.

Consider the answer "Arno dislikes something on every pizza". It is given by $L=\varnothing$ unless some pizza is empty, and by $L=\{T\}$ unless some pizza is contained in $\{T\}$. Suppose no pizza is empty. Then $L=\varnothing$ gives this answer, so for each topping $T$ the set $L=\{T\}$ must not give it: some pizza is $\subseteq\{T\}$, hence equals $\{T\}$. Doing this for all five toppings, the five pizzas are exactly $\{T\}$ for the five toppings $T$ (each pizza is a different singleton, since five singletons are required among five pizzas).

If some pizza were empty, its answer is always "no problem" and carries no information, so only four pizzas give information: at most $2^4=16<32$ answer patterns, which cannot distinguish all $32$ possible sets $L$.

Conversely, with the five single-topping pizzas, the answers tell Purineqa exactly which toppings Arno likes.

**Answer: the five pizzas must each contain exactly one topping, all different (mushrooms, olives, green peppers, cheese, pepperoni).**

hmmt-feb-2012-team1-06.title: Make the pond equilateral
hmmt-feb-2012-team1-06.body:
Apply the linear map $\varphi(x,y)=\left(x+\frac y2,\frac{\sqrt3}2y\right)$. It sends $(0,0),(2012,0),(0,2012)$ to $(0,0)$, $(2012,0)$, $\left(1006,1006\sqrt3\right)$, the vertices of an equilateral triangle $\Delta$, and the integer lattice $\mathbb Z^2$ to the triangular lattice $\Lambda$ generated by $(1,0)$ and $\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$. The three hops become
$$\left(\tfrac32,\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\right),\quad\left(-\tfrac32,\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\right),\quad\left(0,-\sqrt3\right),$$
three vectors of length $\sqrt3$ pointing in directions $30^\circ,150^\circ,270^\circ$, i.e. $120^\circ$ apart.

**Rotate.** Let $\rho$ be the rotation by $120^\circ$ about the center of $\Delta$ that sends the vertex $\varphi(0,0)$ to the vertex $\varphi(0,2012)$ (and permutes the three vertices cyclically). It maps $\Delta$ onto itself. It also maps $\Lambda$ onto itself: write $\rho(p)=\rho(v)+R(p-v)$ for a vertex $v\in\Lambda$, where $R$ is the $120^\circ$ rotation about the origin; $\rho(v)$ is another vertex, hence in $\Lambda$, and $R$ maps the generators of $\Lambda$ into $\Lambda$ (for instance $R(1,0)=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)-(1,0)$). Finally $R$ permutes the three hop vectors. So $\rho$ is a bijection from lattice points of the pond to lattice points of the pond that carries hops to hops. Therefore it maps the set of points Jeff can reach from $(0,0)$ bijectively onto the set of points reachable from $\rho(0,0)$, which is Kenny's start. Hence the two sets have the same size. ∎

hmmt-feb-2012-team1-07.title: Bipyramid over a triangle
hmmt-feb-2012-team1-07.body:
By Radon's theorem the five points split into two parts whose convex hulls meet. If the split is $1+4$, one point lies in the tetrahedron of the other four and the hull is a tetrahedron, whose volume is at most $\frac{8\sqrt3}{27}<\frac{\sqrt3}2$ (a tetrahedron $ABCX$ inscribed in a unit sphere with plane $ABC$ at distance $t$ from the center has $[ABC]\le\frac{3\sqrt3}4(1-t^2)$ and height $\le1+t$, so $V\le\frac{\sqrt3}4(1-t^2)(1+t)\le\frac{8\sqrt3}{27}$, the maximum at $t=\frac13$).

If the split is $2+3$, call the points $A,B,C,X,Y$ so that segment $XY$ meets triangle $ABC$. Then $X,Y$ are on opposite sides of plane $ABC$ and the hull is the union of the tetrahedra $ABCX$ and $ABCY$, so
$$V=\frac13[ABC]\,(d_X+d_Y),$$
where $d_X,d_Y$ are the distances from $X,Y$ to the plane. If the plane is at distance $t$ from the center, then $d_X+d_Y\le2$ (the two points are at most at the two ends of the diameter perpendicular to the plane, which are $1-t$ and $1+t$ from the plane), and the triangle lies in a circle of radius $\sqrt{1-t^2}$ so $[ABC]\le\frac{3\sqrt3}4(1-t^2)\le\frac{3\sqrt3}4$. Hence
$$V\le\frac13\cdot\frac{3\sqrt3}4\cdot2=\frac{\sqrt3}2,$$
with equality when $ABC$ is an equilateral triangle inscribed in a great circle and $X,Y$ are the poles.

**Answer: $\dfrac{\sqrt3}2$**

hmmt-feb-2012-team1-08.title: A bijection
hmmt-feb-2012-team1-08.body:
**The condition on $f$.** Taking $j=i+1$ shows $f(k+1)-f(k)\le1$ for all $k$; conversely, summing these inequalities gives $f(j)-f(i)\le j-i$. So $A(m,n)$ counts sequences $f(1),\dots,f(n)\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ with $f(k+1)\le f(k)+1$ for each $k$.

**The paths.** A function $g$ is a $\pm1$ path of length $2n+m$ from $0$ to $m$ staying in $[0,m]$. With $u$ up steps and $d$ down steps, $u+d=2n+m$ and $u-d=m$, so $d=n$. Let the down steps be the steps number $i_1<\dots<i_n$ and let $h_j=g(i_j-1)$ be the height just before the $j$-th down step. Then $1\le h_j\le m$ (the path must stay $\ge0$ after the down step). After the $j$-th down step the height is $h_j-1$ and only up steps follow until the next down step, so $h_{j+1}\ge h_j-1$. Conversely, given any sequence $h_1,\dots,h_n\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ with $h_{j+1}\ge h_j-1$, build the path: go up $h_1$ steps, down, go up to $h_2$, down, and so on, and after the last down step go up to $m$ (possible since $h_n-1\le m$). It stays in $[0,m]$ and has the required endpoints, and the construction is inverse to the previous one. So paths $g$ correspond bijectively to sequences $(h_j)$ in $\{1,\dots,m\}^n$ with $h_{j+1}\ge h_j-1$.

**The bijection.** Put $f(j)=m+1-h_j\in\{1,\dots,m\}$. Then $h_{j+1}\ge h_j-1\iff f(j+1)\le f(j)+1$, exactly the condition for $A(m,n)$. This is a bijection between the objects counted by $B(m,n)$ and by $A(m,n)$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2012-team1-09.title: Farey sequence
hmmt-feb-2012-team1-09.body:
Let $\frac{b_1}{a_1}<\frac{b_2}{a_2}<\dots<\frac{b_{M}}{a_{M}}$ be all fractions in lowest terms with $0\le\frac ba\le1$ and denominator $a\le n$ (the Farey sequence of order $n$), so $\frac{b_1}{a_1}=\frac01$, $\frac{b_M}{a_M}=\frac11$. For $k\ge2$ the denominator $k$ occurs $\varphi(k)$ times and $1$ occurs twice (as $\frac01$ and $\frac11$), so $M=N+1$.

**Key fact.** For consecutive terms, $b_{i+1}a_i-b_ia_{i+1}=1$. Indeed, consider the lattice triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(a_i,b_i)$, $(a_{i+1},b_{i+1})$. The sides from the origin contain no other lattice points (the fractions are in lowest terms), and a lattice point $(a,b)$ on the third side or inside the triangle would have $a\le\max(a_i,a_{i+1})\le n$ and slope $b/a$ strictly between the two consecutive fractions, whose reduced form would be another term of the Farey sequence between them, a contradiction. So by Pick's theorem the area is $0+\frac32-1=\frac12$, but this area is $\frac12\left(b_{i+1}a_i-b_ia_{i+1}\right)$. Hence
$$\frac1{a_ia_{i+1}}=\frac{b_{i+1}}{a_{i+1}}-\frac{b_i}{a_i}.$$

**The sequence.** Take $a_1,\dots,a_N$ to be the denominators of the first $N$ fractions. It has exactly $\varphi(k)$ copies of each $k\le n$ (we dropped only the final $\frac11$, so the denominator $1$ appears once $=\varphi(1)$). Since $a_1=a_{N+1}=1$,
$$\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac1{a_ia_{i+1}}\ \ (\text{indices cyclic, } a_{N+1}=a_1=1)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\frac{b_{i+1}}{a_{i+1}}-\frac{b_i}{a_i}\right)=\frac{b_{N+1}}{a_{N+1}}-\frac{b_1}{a_1}=1-0=1.\ ∎$$

hmmt-feb-2012-team1-10.title: Reduce to round-robin tournaments
hmmt-feb-2012-team1-10.body:
**The diagonal.** Each symbol $i$ appears $n$ times in $A$; off the diagonal its occurrences come in symmetric pairs, so it appears an even number of times off the diagonal and hence an odd number of times on the diagonal. The diagonal has $n$ entries and each of the $n$ symbols appears at least once on it, so each appears exactly once: the diagonal is a permutation. Renaming the symbols so that the diagonal reads $1,2,\dots,n$ is a bijection onto "good" matrices (diagonal $1,\dots,n$), and each good matrix arises from exactly $n!$ matrices. So $f(n)=n!\,g(n)$ where $g(n)$ is the number of good matrices, and we must show $g(n)\ge rac{(n-1)!}{\varphi(n)}$.

**Good matrices = tournaments.** Consider round-robin tournaments among teams $1,\dots,n$ played over $n$ days, where on day $k$ team $k$ is idle and the other $n-1$ teams are paired up ($ rac{n-1}2$ matches), and every pair of teams meets exactly once. Given a good matrix, let teams $i
e j$ meet on day $A_{ij}$. Each row contains each value once, so team $i$ plays on each day except day $A_{ii}=i$, exactly once; every pair meets once because $A$ is symmetric. Conversely, a tournament gives a good matrix by $A_{ij}=$ the day $i$ and $j$ meet and $A_{kk}=k$. These are inverse bijections. So $g(n)$ is the number of such tournaments.

**Many tournaments.** Place the vertices of a regular $n$-gon at the points $0,1,\dots,n-1$ of $\mathbb Z_n$ and let $\lambda$ be any bijection from the teams to the vertices ($n!$ choices). Define the tournament $T_\lambda$: on the day of team $k$, pair up the other vertices symmetrically about the vertex $\lambda(k)$ (the pairs $\{\lambda(k)+d,\lambda(k)-d\}$, $d=1,\dots, rac{n-1}2$). Since $n$ is odd, two vertices $x
e y$ have a unique midpoint $z= rac{x+y}2\in\mathbb Z_n$, so every pair meets exactly once. Thus $T_\lambda$ is a valid tournament.

**How often a tournament arises.** Suppose $T_\lambda=T_{\lambda'}$ and let $\mu=\lambda'\circ\lambda^{-1}$, a permutation of $\mathbb Z_n$. Teams $u,w$ meet on the day of team $k$ iff $\lambda(u)+\lambda(w)=2\lambda(k)$ iff $\lambda'(u)+\lambda'(w)=2\lambda'(k)$. Hence for all $x
e y$: $x+y=2z\Rightarrow\mu(x)+\mu(y)=2\mu(z)$. Put $
u(x)=\mu(x)-\mu(0)$. Taking $y=-x$, $z=0$ gives $
u(-x)=-
u(x)$; taking $y=0$ gives $
u(x)=2
u(x/2)$ (division by $2$ is possible in $\mathbb Z_n$); so for all $x,y$, $
u(x)+
u(y)=2
u\left( rac{x+y}2ight)=
u(x+y)$. Thus $
u$ is additive, $
u(x)=ax$ with $a=
u(1)$, and since $\mu$ is a bijection $a$ is a unit mod $n$. So $\mu(x)=ax+b$ with $b\in\mathbb Z_n$, $\gcd(a,n)=1$: at most $n\varphi(n)$ choices. So each tournament arises from at most $n\varphi(n)$ bijections $\lambda$, and the number of distinct tournaments is at least
$$ rac{n!}{n\,\varphi(n)}= rac{(n-1)!}{\varphi(n)}.$$
Hence $g(n)\ge rac{(n-1)!}{\varphi(n)}$ and $f(n)=n!\,g(n)\ge rac{n!\,(n-1)!}{\varphi(n)}$. ∎
